                                     PUC DOCKET NO. 59475
                               SOAH DOCKET NO. 473-26-16349



APPLICATION OF ONCOR ELECTRIC                             §
DELIVERY COMPANY LLC AND LCRA                             §                  BEFORE THE
TRANSMISSION SERVICES CORPORATION                         §
TO AMEND THEIR CERTIFICATES OF                            §              THE STATE OFFICE
CONVENIENCE AND NECESSITY FOR THE                         §
BELL COUNTY EAST SWITCH TO BIG HILL                       §                        OF
SUBSTATION 765-KV TRANSMISSION LINE                       §
PROJECT IN BELL, BURNET, CONCHO,                          §               ADMINISTRATIVE
CORYELL, LAMPASAS, LLANO, MASON,                          §
MCCULLOCH, MENARD, MILAM, MILLS,                          §                   HEARINGS
SAN SABA, SCHLEICHER, TOM GREEN,                          §
AND WILLIAMSON COUNTIES                                   §



                  KEVIN KENNEDY’S INITIAL POST-HEARING BRIEF



        Kevin Kennedy ("Mr. Kennedy”) timely files this Initial Brief to the State Office of

Administrative Hearings ("SOAH") Administrative Law Judges ("ALJs") regarding Oncor

Electric Delivery Company LLC’s (“Oncor’s”) and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation’s

(“LCRA’s”)(collectively, “Applicants’”) application for a certificate of convenience and

necessity (“CCN”) for Bell County East to Bill Hill 765-kV transmission line.

        Mr. Kennedy respectfully requests the SOAH ALJs and the Commission to properly and

rightfully determine this application does not meet PURA requirements and to therefore find the

application must be DENIED. Please, do not give the Applicants the State’s heavy hammer of

eminent domain authority and allow them to use that hammer to beat down the fine citizens and

landowners of Central Texas based on an application that is so lacking in every regard.




KENNEDY 59475 – Initial Post-Hearing Brief                                                Page 1 of 35
                                          I. INTRODUCTION

The evidence has shown the ALJs should recommend DENIAL of the application, and the

Commission should ultimately DENY the application due to the following, which this brief later

discusses in greater detail.

DENY THE APPLICANTS’ APPLICATION DUE TO:


   Applicant’s failure to demonstrate the necessity of the project:

        o Applicants’ failure to describe a numeric, quantifiable and actionable need regarding

            the amount of power needing to be transferred (MW of import needed), as required

            by PURA 37.056.(a) and Question 14. Need for the Proposed Project of the

            application. [Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 1, Application at pp.19-24]

        o Applicants’ failure to describe a numeric, quantifiable and specific power transfer rate

            that the project delivers (MW of import provided) to address a quantifiable need, as

            required by PURA 37.056.(a) and Question 14. Need for the Proposed Project of the

            application. [Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 1, Application at pp.19-24]

        o Applicants’ failure to provide any proof, or indicate in any manner, that despite the

            documented deficit of supply in the Central Texas Corridor, that there is a reliable

            surplus of supply as necessary to address any import capability to Big Hill and Sand

            Lake from Bell County East, as required PURA 37.056.(a) and issue 14. Need for the

            Proposed Project of the application. [Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 1, Application at p.19-24]

   Applicant’s failure to afford opportunity for public meeting, obtain adequate community

    value input and collect property owner input and constraint data:




KENNEDY 59475 – Initial Post-Hearing Brief                                                  Page 2 of 35
         o Applicants’ failure to properly notify affected landowners of the project and afford

             opportunity to attend a public meeting, for all landowners who would be affected by

             the eventual application, as required by 16 TAC 22.52.(a).(4).

        o Applicants’ concealment of approximately 400 miles of route links, impacting over

             1,300 properties, until the filing of their application when it was far too late for those

             affected property owners to adequately and meaningfully exercise their right to

             participate during the project planning phase, describe constraints, provide input

             regarding community values PURA 37.056.(c).(4).(A), and otherwise protect their

             interests and property, as required by 16 TAC 22.52.(a).(4).

   Applicant’s failure to properly notify affected landowners and violations of due process

    rights

        o The Applicants’ failure to obtain the current county tax rolls for use in establishing

             the mailing address of the current owners of affected properties and resulting failure

             to notify certain affected landowners of the application, as required by 16 TAC

             22.52.(a).(3).

        o Violation of the due process protections of the 5th Amendment to the Constitution of

             the United States, which provides inalienable protections including notice,

             opportunity to be heard, right to cross-examine, right to a thorough examination of

             the evidence, and right to counsel.

        o The 4th Amendment to the Constitution of the United States provides protection

             against seizure of property when the 5th Amendment due process rights have been

             violated. The State and its assigns will be denied the use of eminent domain in this

             matter due to 5th Amendment violations that have occurred during this proceeding.




KENNEDY 59475 – Initial Post-Hearing Brief                                                   Page 3 of 35
    Applicants’ failure to comply with PURA 37.056.(c).(4).(A) requirement to consider

    community values.

   Applicants’ failure to comply with Commission policy of prudent avoidance:

        o Applicants’ failure to properly, adequately, and accurately describe the sites they

            considered habitable structures (“HABs”), as required by Question 21. Habitable

            Structures of the application. [Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 1, Application at pp.35-36]

        o Applicants’ failure to disclose in their application that they included travel trailers in

            their list of HABs, even though a travel trailer’s location is temporary in nature and

            are certainly not permanent of semi-permanent structures. Listing undisclosed travel

            trailers as a HABs is in violation of 16 TAC 25.101.(a).(3) and Question 21.

            Habitable Structures of the application, which require a general description of each

            HAB.

        o Applicants’ flawed analysis, evaluation and comparison of proposed routes to one

            another due to Applicants’ erroneous habitable structure summary and erroneous

            number of HABs indicated as being in 520-foot proximity on each route. The number

            of true HABs impacted along each route remains unknown.

        o Applicants’ failure to disclose in their application that they placed proposed route link

            F34 only 395 feet from the Florence Elementary School, exposing over 500 little kids

            to electric and magnetic fields, in violation of 16 TAC 25.101.(b).(3).(B).(iv) [Oncor &

            LCRA TSC Ex. 1A, Application Errata at p.352].

        o Applicants’ failure to perform and provided any evidence of any reasonable

            investments, whatsoever, of money and effort to avoid the Florence Elementary

            School.




KENNEDY 59475 – Initial Post-Hearing Brief                                                     Page 4 of 35
    Applicants’ failure to consider “fatal-flaw” constraints and to inform the Commission of such

    constraints in their application

        o Applicants’ failure to disclose in their application that they placed proposed route link

            F34 only 395 feet from the Florence Elementary School, exposing over 500 little kids

            to electric and magnetic fields, in violation of 16 TAC 25.101.(b).(3).(B).(iv).

        o Applicants’ witness, environmental scientist, senior project manager and QA/QC

            person, Russell Masurak, testified they performed field reconnaissance and identified

            the Florence Elementary School in June 2025, [Hearing Transcript, Monday, June 8, 2026,

            Masurak testimony at p.103:13-25, p.104:22-25, p.105:1-3, p.106:14-25 and p.107:1-8] yet this

            person of lofty title with critical responsibilities related to the project’s production and

            QA/QC failed to cause any proper identification or take prudent action regarding the

            Florence Elementary School.

        o Applicants’ failure to disclose in their application that they placed proposed route link

            F34 though the middle of Williamson County’s proposed five-level interchange at SH

            195 and Corridor J, in disregard and violation of 16 TAC 25.101.(b).(3).(B) (routing –

            engineering constraints) [JKK Poole EX 14, SH 195 – Corridor J Interchange]

   Applicants’ unreasonably aggressive plan to clear-cut the entire 200-foot ROW easement

    width on private property [Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 1, EA 1.3.3 at p.67], when clear-cutting is not

    required, is against all things good and decent, and is opposed by PUC staff. Mr. Poole

    recommends the Applicants lay lightly on the land and minimize the amount of flora and

    fauna disturbed during construction. [Staff Ex 1, Poole Direct at p.21:8-16]

   Applicants’ consultants’ apparent failure to exercise the ordinary standard of care, expected

    of reasonably prudent members of their profession, practicing under similar circumstances

    and in the same or similar locality, with respect to being careful, diligent, and competent,


KENNEDY 59475 – Initial Post-Hearing Brief                                                         Page 5 of 35
     providing overall accuracy and completeness of the planning process and application, as well

    as the quality assurance and quality control for a project of this scope, scale and cost, as

    evidenced by the numerous errors and omissions in the application, as listed above, and those

    yet undiscovered, as required by 22 TAC §137.63.

   Applicant’s overall cost overruns and failure to account for all reasonably calculable costs,

    such as cathodic protection of pipelines. These costs are anticipated in certain route links but

    have not been included in the evaluation. This skews the decision making process and creates

    an unknown where there should be none.




                                             II. ARGUMENTS

    1. Need for the construction and ability to address any need not established: PURA

        37.054.(c).(3)

            a. It is not the duty or burden of landowner intervenors to prove the project is not

                needed. Applicants are required to prove necessity in their application for CCN at

                Question 14. Need for the Proposed Project [Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 1, Application at

                p.19] to “describe the need for the construction and state how the proposed project

                will address the need”

            b. The Applicants’ application relies wholly and solely on two documents to attempt

                to describe the need and the project’s ability to address the need, those being

                HB5066(88) [Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 17, Gurley Rebuttal at pp.24-26] and the Permian

                Basin Reliability Plan (“PBRP”). [Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 3, Gurley Direct at pp.34-105]

                    i. HB5066 did not authorize or require this transmission line project. The

                         Applicants’ application misrepresents the HB5066 text when they state



KENNEDY 59475 – Initial Post-Hearing Brief                                                 Page 6 of 35
                         HB5066 required the Commission to direct ERCOT to develop a plan to

                        accomplish “(2) increase available transmission capacity to meet

                        forecasted load”. [Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 1, Application at p.19]

                   ii. The truth is HB5066 does not require an increase in transmission. It is an

                        irrefutable fact that HB5066 simply requires a plan to “(2) address

                        increasing available capacity to meet forecasted load”. [Oncor & LCRA TSC

                        Ex. 17, Gurley Rebuttal at p.26:18-27]

            c. Applicants appear to attempt to create a project “benefit” from thin air with an

                unsubstantiated interjection in the application that the project “will improve bi-

                directional power flow on the ERCOT transmission system”. [Oncor & LCRA TSC

                Ex. 1, Application at p.24] This is the only mention of “bi-directional flow” in the

                entire application. If this was a key component or need of the project, as the

                Applicants appear to claim, then HB5066 and the PBRP would have clearly

                identified it as such. They do not.

                    i. HB5066 and ERCOT’s PBRP, which the Applicants rely on exclusively

                        for project need, are laser focused on moving power in only one direction,

                        importing to the Permian from the east; not the other direction.

                   ii. After at least fifteen months of work preparing the application, the

                        Applicants provided no evidence in the application of their claimed benefit

                        or existence “bi-directional flow”. This apparent mischaracterization of

                        need is indicative of the lack of quality and accuracy of the application

                        and is purely another red herring.

                   iii. Neither HB5066 nor the PBRP, which are the entire basis for the

                        application’s evidence of need, make any mention whatsoever of bi-


KENNEDY 59475 – Initial Post-Hearing Brief                                                    Page 7 of 35
                         directional power flow. The PBRP references only the IMPORT or transfer

                        of power from Bell County East to Big Hill and Sand Lake. If the

                        Applicant believed “bi-directional flow” was an important aspect of the

                        project, information describing the analysis and validation of such a claim

                        should have been included in the application, but it was not.

            d. PBRP and the application never provides or defines a quantifiable or actionable

                need at Sand Lake or Big Hill. [Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 3, Gurley Direct at pp.34-105]

                    i. Neither the application or the PBRP ever define an actual need at Big Hill,

                        Sand Lake or anywhere in the Permian.

                   ii. PBRP simply shows a claimed forecast of future total load demand for the

                        entire Permian Basin of 23,659-MW (2030) and 26,400-MW 2038) [Oncor

                        & LCRA TSC Ex. 3, Gurley Direct at p.56] but it never provides the initial

                        available supply. Without the initial available supply, the resulting actual

                        need of new or additional, as required by PURA 37.056.(a), is

                        indeterminate.

                   iii. The net supply deficit (need) is never defined for the Permian, as a whole.

                   iv. The net supply deficit (need) for Sand Lake is never defined.

                    v. The net supply deficit (need) for Big Hill is never defined.

                   vi. After reading the PBRP, one would have no ability to discern any

                        quantifiable and actionable need, at any specific location, nor within the

                        vast Permian Basin as a whole. The PBRP never provides the exact

                        amount of MW needed to address the supposed deficit at Sand Lake or

                        Big Hill.




KENNEDY 59475 – Initial Post-Hearing Brief                                                    Page 8 of 35
                   vii. The PBRP and its so-called “recommendations” are arbitrary and

                        capricious.

                 viii. The PBRP is not an engineering study, with irrefutable facts and figures. It

                        is simply a loose planning document with generalized statements,

                        ambiguities and hyperbole. PBRP may be sufficient to guide decisions

                        regarding the need for future, detailed engineering studies, but it has no

                        foundational engineering that would qualify it to stand as the sole basis for

                        a Commission decision to authorize eminent domain authority and rate-

                        payer liability for construction of $4-billion, 400-mile scar across Central

                        Texas, that likely does not and cannot serve the generic purpose stated in

                        the application, which is only to take power from east to west, without

                        quantification, as required by PURA 37.056.

                   ix. The recommendations of the PBRP are akin to someone saying, “We need

                        a lot of water in Texas in the future” and expecting that anyone could

                        respond to and satisfy that supposed statement of need with a specific

                        project or set of projects to address that need. How much water, where, is

                        there a reliable source, etc., etc.? These necessary questions are asked by

                        the Commission’s CCN application and review process but the Applicants

                        and their application have not answered them.

                    x. If I need ten gallons of water, but I already have six gallons, my true,

                        actionable need is four gallons. If you do not know my true need, you

                        cannot address it. If you propose to sell me a one-gallon bucket, that is

                        insufficient to address my true need. If you propose to sell me a tanker-

                        truck, you are wasting my money. Since ERCOT did not define the true


KENNEDY 59475 – Initial Post-Hearing Brief                                                Page 9 of 35
                         four-gallon need, the Applicants cannot propose to sell the rate-payers a

                        “right-sized” bucket.

                   xi. The Applicants have no idea what ERCOT’s alleged need is. Applicants

                        have no idea how many megawatts are needed at Big Hill or how many

                        megawatts are needed at Sand Lake; if they do, why have they not told us?

                  xii. If they know the need and it is hidden somewhere in their application,

                        let them point it out to us in their Reply Brief.

                 xiii. When asked for this very information, Mr. Gurley has said repeatedly that

                        the Applicants did not perform the PBRP study and that they do not know

                        the details. [Kennedy Ex. N20, RFI 9 at pp.4-8]

            e. No quantifiable ability to address a defined need

                    i. The available supply of reliable power (ability to address need) in Bell

                        County East is never defined or addressed in any manner by the

                        Applicants or the PBRP.

                   ii. The Applicant and PBRP never indicate the amount of power, if any, that

                        flows through Import Path 2 from Bell County East to Big Hill and/or

                        Sand Lake.

                   iii. When asked for this very information, Mr. Gurley has said repeatedly that

                        the Applicants did not perform the PBRP study and that they do not know

                        the details. [Kennedy Ex. N20, RFI 9 at pp.4-8]

                   iv. Without knowing the power flow, it is impossible to justify any sized

                        transmission line or a transmission project at all. Why a 765-kV line? Why

                        not a 138-kV or why not nothing at all? The Applicant and ERCOT never

                        justify or attempt to explain the project, not in the least. They simply say


KENNEDY 59475 – Initial Post-Hearing Brief                                                Page 10 of 35
                         we need a lot of power in the Permian, which is insufficient and far too

                        flimsy a justification for the foundation of a Commission decision on such

                        a large and impactful project.

                    v. Without a reliable source for the four-gallons of water needed above, a

                        bucket that is simply a transport device has no value. This is analogous to

                        what we have here. No description of actual need, no justification for the

                        size of the bucket (transmission line), no acknowledgment or resolution of

                        the known, long-standing and studied supply deficit identified by the

                        2023-RTP, 2024-RTP and 2025-RTP for the Central Texas Corridor has

                        been addressed and resolved. [Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 17, 2024-RTP at p.32 (last

                        paragraph) and 2025-RTP at p.77 (middle of page)]

            f. Central Texas Corridor has no surplus power to divert to Permian

                    i. 2023, 2024 and 2025-RTPs all state there is an ongoing shortage of power

                        in the Central Texas Corridor, which includes Bell County. [Oncor & LCRA

                        TSC Ex. 17, 2024-RTP at p.32 (last paragraph) and 2025-RTP at p.77 (middle of page)]

                   ii. 2025-RTP recommends that construction of a 130-mile, 765-kV line to

                        import 2,000-MW of power from Gulf Coast to Central Texas Corridor, in

                        an attempt to remedy the shortage of power in the Central Texas Corridor.

                        . [Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 17, 2025-RTP at p.104] It is obvious by these ERCOT

                        studies that there is no surplus of reliable power in the Central Texas

                        Corridor, which includes Bell County, to supply power to Import Path 2 so

                        it may be carried west to Big Hill and Sand Lake.

                   iii. Applicants and PBRP never address this obvious supply deficiency or

                        define the supposed origin of power presumably supplied to Big Hill and



KENNEDY 59475 – Initial Post-Hearing Brief                                                      Page 11 of 35
                         Sand Lake through Import Path 2, or how much power is actually

                        imported from Bell County East to Big Hill and Sand Lake.

                   iv. Without this information, the ability of the project to address need, is not

                        established.

            g. The forecasted TSP loads used to justify Import Path 2 in the PBRP have been

                debunked, determined to be exaggerated, and have been and are continuing to be

                slashed to a fraction of the loads relied upon to justify the PBRP

                recommendations.

                    i. June 5, 2025 Good Cause Exception to reduce load. [PUC Docket 55999-142]

                   ii. May 18, 2026 ERCOT load reduction request [PUC Docket 59772-1]

                   iii. June 1, 2026 Office of Public Utilities Counsel’s comments supporting

                        ERCOT’s load reduction request [PUC Docket 59772-14]

            h. Input must be accurate and consistent to obtain accurate and consistent results

                    i. The PBRP and the 2024-RTP, which were developed concurrently by

                        ERCOT during 2024, do not appear to have same modeling topology input

                        variables and possibly have different transmission network configurations.

                        By using different models, ERCOT receives differing results. This begs

                        the question of why would ERCOT develop concurrent models over the

                        course of 2024? Why not utilize a single topology model? Did they find

                        one set of results from the PBRP model and another set of results the 24-

                        RTP model?

                   ii. The differences in the two models appear too numerous and too significant

                        to ignore.




KENNEDY 59475 – Initial Post-Hearing Brief                                               Page 12 of 35
                             1. In an RFI, Mr. Gurley was asked several questions about the

                                differences in the topology modeling utilized in the PBRP, 2024-

                                RTP, and 2025_RTP. He repeatedly responded that “ERCOT, not

                                the Applicants, performed these studies. Therefore, the Applicants

                                do not have this information.” [Kennedy Ex. N23, RFI 16 at pp.6-8] As

                                such, the Applicants have admitted they have no knowledge of the

                                ERCOT models.

                            2. 2024-RTP states there is a deficit in the Central Texas Corridor

                                while PBRP appears to rely on a supposed surplus to justify two

                                765-kV Permian Import Paths (Import 2-Bell Co. & Import 3-

                                Bexar), which combined would be capable of carrying around

                                5,000-MW. [Kennedy Ex. N18, RFI 3 at pp.4-5]

                            3. 2024-RTP utilizes the addition of two gas plants in the Permian,

                                generating 1,850-MW of power, but leaves the three Permian 765-

                                kV import paths with no analysis, while the PBRP claims no

                                additional generation is needed in the Permian. [Oncor & LCRA TSC

                                Ex. 17, 2024-RTP at p.47 and App. B: Tab-Gen Add. Ret. and Mothball]

                            4. 2024-RTP appears to add a total of about 59,200-MW of

                                generation [Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 17, 2024-RTP App. B: Tab-Gen Add.

                                Ret. and Mothball] to its model. PBRP only adds about 17,170-MW,

                                [Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 3, PBRP App. A1 at pp.102-104] with only about

                                8,900-MW of the 17,170-MW also being in the 2024-RTP’s

                                59,000-MW. This appears to make the actual difference in

                                additional generation in the 2024-RTP vs. the PBRP probably


KENNEDY 59475 – Initial Post-Hearing Brief                                                     Page 13 of 35
                                 around 50,900-MW of generation. Why such a significant

                                discrepancy?

                            5. The total load demand in each of the studies would be required

                                closely match the generation to balance the supply/demand

                                amounts so the 2024-RTP would have approximately 50,000-MW

                                more total load demand in its topology model study cases than the

                                PBRP topology models.

                            6. It seems clear that though these two studies were done

                                concurrently, though they are definitely not the same. Given the

                                large disparity in future generation needed to address the

                                forecasted load, the PBRP must have also had a much lower load

                                demand. The PBRP never seems to state the total load demand for

                                the model, but only provides data within the Permian region.

                            7. ERCOT appears to use a lesser load demand in areas outside the

                                Permian in the PBRP than what they used in the concurrently

                                developed 2024-RTP. If so, this would create a false surplus in the

                                east. ERCOT certainly includes less generation in the in the

                                Permian region in the PBRP than what they did in the 2024-RTP.

                                These two factors would seem to create a greater net Permian

                                supply deficiency in the PBRP than would be created in the 2024-

                                RTP. There are many modeling questions that ERCOT should be

                                required to answer, but to date has not.

                            8. A lesser future load demand in East Texas in the PBRP, coupled

                                with les generation in the west, might explain how the PBRP


KENNEDY 59475 – Initial Post-Hearing Brief                                               Page 14 of 35
                                 “finds” available power at Bell County East. Without being able to

                                drill down on the details of the topology model input parameters, it

                                is impossible to determine why supply and demand parameters are

                                different in the two studies and how that affects model analysis,

                                output, accuracy and validity.

                            9. On its face, the PBRP appears to be the epitome of hearsay. The

                                Applicants rely on and use the PBRP to justify their case, but the

                                PBRP provides more questions than answers. ERCOT is not a

                                party to this case, so landowner intervenors have no opportunity to

                                seek discovery or cross-examine ERCOT to ask questions and

                                establish the validity, or lack thereof, of ERCOT’s PBRP topology

                                modeling.

                            10. However, it is not the responsibility of landowner intervenors

                                to disprove need; it is the responsibility of the Applicants to

                                prove need.

                            11. The PBRP should be inadmissible as hearsay and since it is tainted

                                evidence, everything that flows from the PBRP, including the

                                application, is fruit of the poisonous tree.

                            12. Given the intervenors’ inability to cross-examine ERCOT, the total

                                burden of proof of need falls to the Applicants. The Applicants

                                have stated time and time again that they did not perform the

                                studies for the PBRP and have no knowledge of it. [Kennedy Ex. N23,

                                RFI 16 at pp.6-8] As such, the Applicants have failed to establish

                                project need or the ability of the project to address need, as


KENNEDY 59475 – Initial Post-Hearing Brief                                                 Page 15 of 35
                                 required by PURA 37.056.(a) and issue 14. Need for the Proposed

                                Project of the application and they have admitted they have no

                                ability to provide proof of necessity.

    2. Import Path 2 is NOT NEEDED UNTIL 2038;

            a. Everyone, including the Commission and Applicants, can slow down and make

                sure we get this right.

            b. In the 7-25-2024 PBRP, ERCOT indicates Import Path 2 is not needed until 2038.

                [Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 3, PBRP at p.39 (middle of page)] ERCOT restates and reinforces

                this fact in their 12-12-2024 Sequencing Letter to the PUC Commissioners. [JKK

                PANEL EX 01, PBRP Sequencing Letter, at p.2(first paragraph)]. These facts are irrefutable

                and as such, have not been opposed or disproved.

            c. The Applicants attempt to claim that ERCOT reversed course on their 2024 RTP

                findings in one week, between 12-12-2024 and 12-20-2024, on a major study they

                had been working on for almost one year, and at the very last minute decided

                Import Path 2 was needed in 2030, not 2038. The 2024 RTP was a 33-page report

                of an 11-month study, with 17 appendices. That is not the kind of technical

                analysis that flips on a dime, as the Applicants suggest. [Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 17,

                2024-RTP at pp.29-72]

            d. From that extensive report, the only item the Applicants can point to is the

                misleading title on one figure: Figure 18: The 765-kV Core Plan needed in 2030.

                [Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 17, 2024-RTP Fig 18 at p.62]. That’s it, nothing more, because

                there is no more. We know from the Applicants’ own struggles with their

                application that labeling can be tricky, like when they mislabeled a church or an




KENNEDY 59475 – Initial Post-Hearing Brief                                                    Page 16 of 35
                  elementary school as commercial / industrial sites in an important document.

                 [Oncor & LCRA TSC Ex. 1A, Application Errata at pp.348 & 352]

            e.   Let us correctly look to the body of the report to judge the veracity of the

                 Applicants’ claim, rather than relying how a figure is labeled for such crucial

                 information. On the 2024-RTP page preceding Figure 18, ERCOT states “After

                 establishing the core plan, ERCOT developed a 765-kV plan in parallel with the

                 regular 345-kV plan to address the reliability issues identified in the analysis. The

                 RTP 765-kV plan was created using the 2030 summer peak case, which also

                 served as the start case for the 345-kV plan. The start case for the 765-kV plan

                 incorporated all local projects needed by 2030 in the Permian Basin Reliability

                 Plan, along with the three Permian Basin 765-kV import paths.”. [Oncor & LCRA

                 TSC Ex. 17, 2024-RTP at p.61]

            f. ERCOT clearly states they simply added the three Permian Basin 765-kV import

                 paths to the projects needed in 2030 to create what they called the “core plan”.

                 They do not state the three import paths are needed in 2030 but rather they

                 indicate that they added the import paths to the projects needed in 2030 to make

                 the “core plan”. The import paths were incorporated in the core plan but they are
